material: Etching on laid paper backed with japon
provenance: Ambroise Firmin-Didot (Lugt 119) | Galerie Michael, Beverly Hills | Acquired by descent directly from the above | | Lot Essay | Ambroise Firmin-Didot was the son of the publisher Firmin Didot. He was an educated man with a passion for understanding and collecting antiquities. He began collecting Italian prints, which eventually led him to pursue printmaking himself, something he saw as a logical next step in his research on printing. To deepen his understanding of the printing process, he surrounded himself with printers from across Europe, including German masters and French engravers. He became an important collector of antiquities, books, essays, and works by Old Master printmakers such as Dürer and Rembrandt.
subject_matter: prints, antiquities, books, essays, engravings, Italian prints, Old Master printmakers, Dürer, Rembrandt, collectors

provenance: Pace Gallery, New York, March 15, 1991 | Acquired from directly from above by the present owner | | Lot Essay | Venus, the goddess of love and beauty, has become a signature, repeated motif in Jim Dine's work. Throughout his seven-decade career, he has developed and refined his own visual language, embedding his unique style into the Pop Art movement of the 1950s and 1960s. In 1982, Dine first began exploring the subject of Venus de Milo. The American artist decided to alter a small, store-bought plaster replica of the famous Hellenistic sculpture. He transformed the classic form by removing the figurine's head and adding layered textures to the previously smooth surface. This pivotal moment cemented Venus into his visual lexicon as this motif would re-appear in countless of his paintings, drawings, prints and editioned multiples.

provenance: LA Louver, Los Angeles | Acquired directly from above by the present owner | | Lot Essay | Hockney is revered for his curiosity as an artist. While he experimented with traditional media such as printmaking and painting, he also ventured into modern forms like photography. He was particularly intrigued by the contrast between the fixed, static perspective of a photograph and the more fluid, multifaceted way we experience the world in daily life. | | Using a Polaroid camera, Hockney captured multiple viewpoints of a single subject and assembled them into collages. These "joiners," as he called them, disrupted the conventional, singular perspective offered by the camera, favoring instead a more dynamic and holistic representation of the subject. | | In this particular work, the subject is his longtime friend Gregory, shown reading. The collage compels the viewer not to focus solely on Gregory, but to become immersed in the surrounding environment. Although Hockney was initially skeptical of photography as an artistic medium, he began to incorporate traditional printmaking techniques, such as layering, to connect these fractured perspectives. | | Through his photocollages, Hockney revitalized the principles of Cubism by using modern technology to reconstruct everyday scenes from fragmented visuals into dynamic compositions. Each Polaroid is taken individually, with specific intent, contributing to the uniqueness and richness of the final creation.

artwork_title: The Arrival of Spring in Woldgate, East Yorkshire in 2011 (twenty eleven) - 1 January, 2011
material: iPad drawing in colors on wove paper
provenance: LA Louver Gallery, Venice California | Acquired directly from above by present owner | | Lot Essay | Just as Claude Monet recorded the Rouen Cathedral over the course of the four seasons, David Hockney settled in his mother's Bridlington home in 2006, to record the next five springs in Yorkshire. And just as the first collapsible metal paint tube revolutionized plein air painting for Impressionists like Monet, so too would the iPad for contemporary artists like Hockney. He started drawing on his iPhone in 2008, but just two years later, would devote his digital drawing to the iPad. The Arrival of Spring in Woodgate is a series of iPad drawings chronicling various landscapes and floral scenes in which Hockney captures the transition from an icy winter to a blooming spring. The winding road in this drawing is revisited several times throughout this series, each version capturing a new color scheme and a new unfolding of spring. Hockney used the app Brushes to capture this series, the appeal of which was its simplicity. Without any differentiation between an oil paint brush or a watercolor paintbrush, he felt that it was the most honest digital medium. This simplicity allowed Hockney to focus on experimentation, something he is notoriously fond of. The iPad requires no clean up, can be used at night to capture the moonlight, and allows immediacy with his creations. | | In this print, the first of the 2011 series completed on New Year's Day, most of the trees are bare and snow runs down the side of the road. However, the greenery is a swirling sea of orange and red, the autumn grasp having not quite let go. The clear blue through the icy purple mist at the end of the tree-tunnel captures the crisp cold air of an early January day. These works capture not only Hockney's classic imagery but also showcase game-changing innovation in his body of work. On The Arrival of Spring in Woodgate series, Hockney explains that he "had planned to record the Spring arriving in 2011, having observed its arrival for seven years on Woldgate", and when the snow came, he took to his iPad and began drawing in his car.
